claim: In rodent CA1, theta/gamma coupling occurs during exploration.
source: Although theta/gamma coupling in rodent CA1 occurs during exploration and sharp-wave ripples emerge in quiescence, it is less clear that these oscillatory regimes extend to primates.
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on rodent hippocampal oscillations

claim: Sharp-wave ripples emerge in rodent CA1 during quiescence.
source: Although theta/gamma coupling in rodent CA1 occurs during exploration and sharp-wave ripples emerge in quiescence, it is less clear that these oscillatory regimes extend to primates.
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on rodent hippocampal oscillations

claim: It is unclear whether rodent oscillatory regimes extend to primates.
source: Although theta/gamma coupling in rodent CA1 occurs during exploration and sharp-wave ripples emerge in quiescence, it is less clear that these oscillatory regimes extend to primates.
evidence: Statement of uncertainty based on existing literature gaps

claim: In macaque CA1, theta and gamma frequency bands are segregated by behavioral states.
source: We found that, in contrast to rodent oscillations, theta and gamma frequency bands in macaque CA1 were segregated by behavioral states.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: Beta2/gamma (15–70 Hz) had greater power during visual search in macaque CA1.
source: In both stationary and freely moving designs, beta2/gamma (15–70 Hz) had greater power during visual search whereas the theta band (3–10 Hz; peak ~8 Hz) dominated during quiescence and early sleep.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from both stationary and freely moving conditions

claim: The theta band (3–10 Hz; peak ~8 Hz) dominated during quiescence and early sleep in macaque CA1.
source: In both stationary and freely moving designs, beta2/gamma (15–70 Hz) had greater power during visual search whereas the theta band (3–10 Hz; peak ~8 Hz) dominated during quiescence and early sleep.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from both stationary and freely moving conditions

claim: Theta-band amplitude was strongest when beta2/slow gamma (20–35 Hz) amplitude was weakest in macaque CA1.
source: Moreover, theta-band amplitude was strongest when beta2/slow gamma (20–35 Hz) amplitude was weakest, instead occurring along with higher frequencies (60–150 Hz).
evidence: Supported by cross-frequency amplitude correlation analysis

claim: Theta-band amplitude occurred along with higher frequencies (60–150 Hz) in macaque CA1.
source: Moreover, theta-band amplitude was strongest when beta2/slow gamma (20–35 Hz) amplitude was weakest, instead occurring along with higher frequencies (60–150 Hz).
evidence: Supported by cross-frequency amplitude correlation analysis

claim: Spike-field coherence was most frequently seen in three bands: 3–10 Hz, 20–35 Hz, and 60–150 Hz in macaque CA1.
source: Spike-field coherence was most frequently seen in these three bands (3–10 Hz, 20–35 Hz, and 60–150 Hz); however, the theta-band coherence was largely due to spurious coupling during sharp-wave ripples.
evidence: Supported by spike-field coherence analysis of 404 units

claim: Theta-band coherence was largely due to spurious coupling during sharp-wave ripples in macaque CA1.
source: Spike-field coherence was most frequently seen in these three bands (3–10 Hz, 20–35 Hz, and 60–150 Hz); however, the theta-band coherence was largely due to spurious coupling during sharp-wave ripples.
evidence: Supported by comparison of spike-field coherence during SWRs versus residual periods

claim: No intrinsic theta spiking rhythmicity was apparent in macaque CA1.
source: Accordingly, no intrinsic theta spiking rhythmicity was apparent.
evidence: Supported by spike autocorrelogram analysis showing near-zero theta modulation index values

claim: Beta2/slow gamma modulation plays a role in CA1 during active exploration in the primate.
source: These results support a role for beta2/slow gamma modulation in CA1 during active exploration in the primate that is decoupled from theta oscillations.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing beta2/gamma power during search and decoupling from theta

claim: Beta2/slow gamma is decoupled from theta oscillations in primate CA1.
source: These results support a role for beta2/slow gamma modulation in CA1 during active exploration in the primate that is decoupled from theta oscillations.
evidence: Supported by cross-frequency coupling analyses showing negative correlation and lack of phase-amplitude coupling

claim: The primate hippocampus differs from the rodent oscillatory canon.
source: The apparent difference to the rodent oscillatory canon calls for a shift in focus of frequency when considering the primate hippocampus.
evidence: Inferred from the contrasting findings between primate and rodent oscillatory patterns

claim: Hippocampal oscillations support cognition by coordinating neural circuit dynamics.
source: Hippocampal oscillations are heralded as canonical examples of how oscillations support cognition by coordinating neural circuit dynamics (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004; Colgin, 2016; Hahn et al., 2019; Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: Behavioral states constrain and entrain specific neural oscillations.
source: In turn, behavioral states constrain and entrain specific neural oscillations.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in neuroscience

claim: In rodents, locomotion and exploratory movements elicit an ~8 Hz theta oscillation in hippocampal CA1.
source: In rodents, locomotion and other exploratory movements elicit an ~8 Hz theta oscillation in hippocampal CA1 (Buzsáki, 2002; Kramis et al., 1975; Vanderwolf, 1969; Whishaw and Vanderwolf, 1973)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to rodent hippocampal literature

claim: In rodents, a faster gamma oscillation (25–100 Hz) nests within theta.
source: In rodents, locomotion and other exploratory movements elicit an ~8 Hz theta oscillation in hippocampal CA1 (Buzsáki, 2002; Kramis et al., 1975; Vanderwolf, 1969; Whishaw and Vanderwolf, 1973) and a faster gamma oscillation (25–100 Hz) that nests within theta (Bragin et al., 1995b; Colgin and Moser, 2010; Colgin, 2016; Csicsvari et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to rodent hippocampal literature

claim: During quiescent states in rodents, theta and gamma oscillations are suppressed.
source: In contrast, during quiescent states, theta and gamma oscillations are suppressed and sharp-wave ripple (SWR) complexes emerge, the latter consisting of large high-frequency oscillations (HFO, 150–250 Hz) in CA1 that occur within a slower (sharp-wave) deflection (Buzsáki, 2015; Ylinen et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent hippocampal literature

claim: Sharp-wave ripple complexes emerge during quiescent states in rodents.
source: In contrast, during quiescent states, theta and gamma oscillations are suppressed and sharp-wave ripple (SWR) complexes emerge, the latter consisting of large high-frequency oscillations (HFO, 150–250 Hz) in CA1 that occur within a slower (sharp-wave) deflection (Buzsáki, 2015; Ylinen et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent hippocampal literature

claim: SWRs consist of large high-frequency oscillations (HFO, 150–250 Hz) in CA1 that occur within a slower (sharp-wave) deflection.
source: In contrast, during quiescent states, theta and gamma oscillations are suppressed and sharp-wave ripple (SWR) complexes emerge, the latter consisting of large high-frequency oscillations (HFO, 150–250 Hz) in CA1 that occur within a slower (sharp-wave) deflection (Buzsáki, 2015; Ylinen et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations defining SWR characteristics

claim: The occurrence of SWRs during quiescence is highly conserved across species.
source: Although the occurrence of SWRs during quiescence is highly conserved across species (Buzsáki, 2015), its dichotomy with theta is questionable (Hussin et al., 2020; Leonard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to comparative neuroscience literature

claim: The dichotomy between SWRs and theta is questionable.
source: Although the occurrence of SWRs during quiescence is highly conserved across species (Buzsáki, 2015), its dichotomy with theta is questionable (Hussin et al., 2020; Leonard et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies questioning the theta-SWR dichotomy

claim: Differences in theta-SWR dichotomy may stem from differences in how and when theta oscillations appear across phylogenetic order.
source: This may stem from differences in how and when theta oscillations appear across phylogenetic order (Green and Arduini, 1954; Ulanovsky and Moss, 2007), particularly among primates, including humans (Courellis et al., 2019; Green and Arduini, 1954; Halgren et al., 1978; Herweg et al., 2020; Jacobs, 2014; Mao et al., 2021 Stewart and Fox, 1991; Talakoub et al., 2019; Tamura et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative studies across species

claim: Gamma coupling to hippocampal theta could be affected by the scarcity of theta oscillations in monkeys during species-relevant exploration.
source: Consequently, gamma coupling to hippocampal theta (Bragin et al., 1995a; Colgin, 2016; Lisman and Jensen, 2013), and the presence – as postulated – of sub-bands of gamma (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Colgin, 2016; Colgin et al., 2009; Csicsvari et al., 2003), could understandably be affected by the scarcity of theta oscillations in monkeys during species-relevant exploration (Courellis et al., 2019; Hoffman et al., 2013; Jutras et al., 2013; Leonard et al., 2015; Mao et al., 2021; Skaggs et al., 2007; Talakoub et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from citations showing scarcity of theta in monkeys and known theta-gamma coupling in rodents

claim: 42 sessions were recorded in the hippocampal CA1 subfield of two macaques during active visual search and quiescence.
source: We recorded 42 sessions (M1: 26 sessions, M2: 16 sessions) in the hippocampal CA1 subfield of two macaques (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) during active visual search and quiescence (henceforth: 'rest').
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design and data collection

claim: Bouts of roughly 20–30 Hz oscillations were observed predominantly during search.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Leonard and Hoffman, 2017; Leonard et al., 2015), we observed bouts of roughly 20–30 Hz oscillations predominantly during search, and slower-frequency, larger-amplitude local field potentials (LFPs) during rest (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and referenced in Figure 1A and C

claim: Slower-frequency, larger-amplitude local field potentials (LFPs) were observed during rest.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Leonard and Hoffman, 2017; Leonard et al., 2015), we observed bouts of roughly 20–30 Hz oscillations predominantly during search, and slower-frequency, larger-amplitude local field potentials (LFPs) during rest (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and referenced in Figure 1A and C

claim: There is an antagonistic relationship between 20–30 Hz and <10 Hz frequencies in macaque CA1.
source: To visualize the relationship between spectral power across frequency bands, we sorted quantiles of ~1 s segments based on their average power in the 20–30 Hz frequency band, revealing an antagonistic relationship between 20–30 Hz and <10 Hz frequencies (Figure 1B), that is when power at 20–30 Hz was greatest, <10 Hz power was qualitatively weakest.
evidence: Supported by spectral analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: When power at 20–30 Hz was greatest, <10 Hz power was qualitatively weakest.
source: To visualize the relationship between spectral power across frequency bands, we sorted quantiles of ~1 s segments based on their average power in the 20–30 Hz frequency band, revealing an antagonistic relationship between 20–30 Hz and <10 Hz frequencies (Figure 1B), that is when power at 20–30 Hz was greatest, <10 Hz power was qualitatively weakest.
evidence: Supported by spectral analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: Stronger power at <10 Hz was accompanied by stronger power at >80 Hz.
source: In contrast, stronger power at <10 Hz was accompanied by stronger power at >80 Hz.
evidence: Supported by spectral analysis

claim: Stronger 7–10 Hz power was found during rest compared to active search.
source: We found stronger 7–10 Hz power during rest compared to active search (Figure 1D, middle).
evidence: Supported by aperiodic-adjusted power spectrum analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: Power in the higher frequencies from 15 Hz to 70 Hz was stronger during active search compared to rest, with a peak in the 20–30 Hz range.
source: In contrast, power in the higher frequencies from 15 Hz to 70 Hz was stronger during active search compared to rest, with a peak in the 20–30 Hz range (both, p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test with FDR correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of power spectra with p<0.05

claim: In most non-rodent species examined, including humans, hippocampal theta-band oscillations during alert wakefulness occur intermittently, in short-lived bouts.
source: In most non-rodent species examined, including humans, hippocampal theta-band oscillations during alert wakefulness are described as occurring intermittently, in short-lived bouts, unlike the protracted and predictable trains of theta oscillations seen in the rodent hippocampus (Green and Arduini, 1954; Jacobs, 2014; Jutras et al., 2013; M Aghajan et al., 2017; Talakoub et al., 2019; Ulanovsky and Moss, 2007; Watrous et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to comparative studies

claim: Rodent hippocampus shows protracted and predictable trains of theta oscillations.
source: In most non-rodent species examined, including humans, hippocampal theta-band oscillations during alert wakefulness are described as occurring intermittently, in short-lived bouts, unlike the protracted and predictable trains of theta oscillations seen in the rodent hippocampus (Green and Arduini, 1954; Jacobs, 2014; Jutras et al., 2013; M Aghajan et al., 2017; Talakoub et al., 2019; Ulanovsky and Moss, 2007; Watrous et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent hippocampal literature

claim: Theta bouts were more prevalent during rest/sleep compared to online active behavioral states.
source: Consistent with continuous power spectral results, we found that theta bouts ('hits') were more prevalent during rest/sleep compared to online active behavioral states.
evidence: Supported by BOSC analysis of oscillatory events

claim: Beta2/gamma frequencies were more prevalent during active states.
source: The pattern was the opposite for beta2/gamma frequencies, which were more prevalent during active states (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, p<0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test with FDR correction).
evidence: Supported by BOSC analysis with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: In rodents, the frequency and amplitude of theta oscillation is related to the speed of locomotion.
source: In rodents, the frequency and the amplitude of theta oscillation is related to the speed of locomotion (Buzsáki, 2002; Fuhrmann et al., 2015; McFarland et al., 1975; Sheremet et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent locomotion studies

claim: Theta activity is observed during awake immobile states of alertness in rodents.
source: In rodents, the frequency and the amplitude of theta oscillation is related to the speed of locomotion (Buzsáki, 2002; Fuhrmann et al., 2015; McFarland et al., 1975; Sheremet et al., 2016) although theta activity is also observed during awake immobile states of alertness (Kramis et al., 1975; Sainsbury, 1998; Tai et al., 2012; Vanderwolf, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent behavioral studies

claim: The decrease in theta-band power and the increase in gamma power during active behaviors were not merely due to the immobile state of the animals.
source: The results match those of the previous experiment, thereby demonstrating that the decrease in theta-band power and the increase in gamma power during active behaviors generalize, that is they were not merely due to the immobile state of the animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by freely moving control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Video 1

claim: The duration and consistency of theta bouts during early sleep indicate that the methods are capable of detecting theta oscillations.
source: Furthermore, the duration and consistency of theta bouts during early sleep indicate that these methods (recording sites, electrode signal, and states) are capable of detecting theta oscillations, but that they appear during different epochs than those for recordings in rats and mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Video 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by analysis of theta bout duration and prevalence during sleep

claim: Theta oscillations appear during different epochs in macaques than in rats and mice.
source: Furthermore, the duration and consistency of theta bouts during early sleep indicate that these methods (recording sites, electrode signal, and states) are capable of detecting theta oscillations, but that they appear during different epochs than those for recordings in rats and mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Video 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of behavioral state correlates between species

claim: Power at 3–8 Hz and 20–35 Hz were negatively correlated.
source: Consistent with the qualitative pattern shown in Figure 1B, power at 3–8 Hz and 20–35 Hz were negatively correlated (Figure 1E, p<0.05, using a cluster-based permutation test corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Supported by cross-frequency power correlation analysis with statistical significance

claim: Power in the slower, 3–8 Hz band was positively correlated with that of a much faster, 80–150 Hz band.
source: In addition, power in the slower, 3–8 Hz band was positively correlated with that of a much faster, 80–150 Hz band.
evidence: Supported by cross-frequency power correlation analysis

claim: The 3–8 Hz band was coupled to high frequencies of 95–150 Hz.
source: To estimate phase-amplitude coupling in the LFP, we performed bicoherence analysis (Figure 1F; Giehl et al., 2021; Hyafil, 2015; Kovach et al., 2018), revealing a peak cluster around the 25 Hz frequency range which confirms an interaction between the activity at this frequency and its second harmonic. In addition, the 3–8 Hz band was coupled to high frequencies of 95–150 Hz (p<0.05, cluster-based Monte Carlo statistical test).
evidence: Supported by bicoherence analysis with statistical significance

claim: There was an interaction between activity at 25 Hz and its second harmonic.
source: To estimate phase-amplitude coupling in the LFP, we performed bicoherence analysis (Figure 1F; Giehl et al., 2021; Hyafil, 2015; Kovach et al., 2018), revealing a peak cluster around the 25 Hz frequency range which confirms an interaction between the activity at this frequency and its second harmonic.
evidence: Supported by bicoherence analysis showing peak at 25 Hz

claim: No significant phase-amplitude coupling was found between theta and gamma frequency range.
source: Nevertheless, our bicoherence results showed no significant phase-amplitude coupling between theta and gamma frequency range.
evidence: Supported by bicoherence analysis

claim: Individual cells phase locked to multiple frequencies.
source: Individual cells phase locked to multiple frequencies (Figure 2A; p<0.05, permutation test and Rayleigh test, p<0.05), with the population showing the full range of spike preferred frequencies of modulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by spike-field coherence analysis with statistical tests

claim: The population showed the full range of spike preferred frequencies of modulation.
source: Individual cells phase locked to multiple frequencies (Figure 2A; p<0.05, permutation test and Rayleigh test, p<0.05), with the population showing the full range of spike preferred frequencies of modulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by population-level spike-field coherence analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: SWRs have a non-oscillatory amplitude envelope within the frequency range of 0.1–10 Hz in rodents and non-human primates.
source: One of the caveats of spike-field coherence measures is that they can be sensitive to large amplitude non-periodic deflections. SWRs have a non-oscillatory amplitude envelope within the frequency range of 0.1–10 Hz in rodents and non-human primates (Hussin et al., 2020; Leonard et al., 2015; Maier et al., 2003; Rex et al., 2009; Skaggs et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing SWR properties

claim: SWRs occur in primates during active visual exploration.
source: Furthermore, we previously observed that SWRs occur in primates during active visual exploration (Leonard and Hoffman, 2017; Leonard et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by the authors

claim: The probability of firing of cells increases during SWR events, for putative pyramidal and inhibitory cells alike.
source: Furthermore, we previously observed that SWRs occur in primates during active visual exploration (Leonard and Hoffman, 2017; Leonard et al., 2015) and that the probability of firing of cells increases during these events, for putative pyramidal and inhibitory cells alike (Hussin et al., 2020; Leonard et al., 2015; Skaggs et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing neural activity during SWRs

claim: Coherence at lower frequencies (2–10 Hz) was greater during SWR than in the SWR-removed distributions.
source: At the population level, coherence at lower frequencies (2–10 Hz) was greater during SWR than in the SWR-removed distributions.
evidence: Supported by comparison of spike-field coherence during and outside SWR windows

claim: Higher frequencies (10–200 Hz) maintained a greater coherence outside of the SWR time window.
source: In contrast, the higher frequencies (10–200 Hz) maintained a greater coherence outside of the SWR time window (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of spike-field coherence during and outside SWR windows shown in Figure 2D

claim: Removing the influence of SWRs led to weaker mean spike-field coherence restricted to the <10 Hz range.
source: This led to weaker mean spike-field coherence restricted to the <10 Hz range, after removing the influence of SWRs, suggesting a contribution of the non-oscillatory slow deflections in the SWR complex to the apparent cross-frequency interactions.
evidence: Supported by analysis comparing spike-field coherence with and without SWR epochs

claim: Non-oscillatory slow deflections in the SWR complex contribute to the apparent cross-frequency interactions.
source: This led to weaker mean spike-field coherence restricted to the <10 Hz range, after removing the influence of SWRs, suggesting a contribution of the non-oscillatory slow deflections in the SWR complex to the apparent cross-frequency interactions.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in low-frequency coherence after SWR removal

claim: Periodic peaks of the spike autocorrelograms demonstrate theta rhythmicity in rat and mouse CA1.
source: Periodic peaks of the spike autocorrelograms demonstrate theta rhythmicity in rat and mouse CA1 (Cacucci et al., 2004; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Royer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent electrophysiology studies

claim: Compared to modulations seen in the rat, monkey cells typically showed near zero theta modulation index values.
source: Compared to modulations seen in the rat (Figure 3B in gray), monkey cells typically showed near zero index values, that is, they were not modulated (Figure 3B in black).
evidence: Supported by theta modulation index analysis comparing monkey and rat data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The most prominent oscillation in amplitude and prevalence during alert active behavior was in the beta2/slow gamma band (~20–35 Hz for stationary search and ~20–50 Hz in freely moving subjects).
source: The most prominent oscillation in amplitude and prevalence during alert active behavior was in the beta2/slow gamma band (~20–35 Hz for stationary search and ~20–50 Hz in freely moving subjects).
evidence: Supported by power spectral analysis and BOSC analysis across behavioral conditions

claim: Theta-band (3–10 Hz, peak at ~8 Hz) amplitude and bout prevalence were greater during offline states of rest and sleep than during online active states.
source: In contrast, theta-band (3–10 Hz, peak at ~8 Hz) amplitude and bout prevalence were greater during offline states of rest and sleep than during online active states.
evidence: Supported by power spectral analysis and BOSC analysis across behavioral states

claim: Theta and beta2/gamma bands were decorrelated in the cross-frequency amplitude coupling.
source: This bimodal oscillatory profile was also evident in finer temporal scales. Theta and beta2/gamma bands were decorrelated in the cross-frequency amplitude coupling, and in phase-amplitude bicoherence, quite unlike that observed in rodents (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cross-frequency amplitude correlation and bicoherence analyses

claim: Theta and beta2/gamma bands were decorrelated in phase-amplitude bicoherence.
source: This bimodal oscillatory profile was also evident in finer temporal scales. Theta and beta2/gamma bands were decorrelated in the cross-frequency amplitude coupling, and in phase-amplitude bicoherence, quite unlike that observed in rodents (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by bicoherence analysis

claim: Only the theta-band spike-field effect appeared to be partially due to non-oscillatory field events, such as the SWR.
source: Spike modulation by LFP frequency was seen in both bands; however, only the theta-band effect appeared to be partially due to non-oscillatory field events, such as the SWR.
evidence: Supported by comparison of spike-field coherence with and without SWR epochs

claim: Overall, no clear evidence of theta-periodic modulation was found despite longer and more prevalent theta oscillations in rest.
source: Despite longer and more prevalent theta oscillations in rest, overall, we found no clear evidence of theta-periodic modulation.
evidence: Supported by spike autocorrelogram analysis showing lack of theta rhythmicity

claim: The same analysis methods applied to signal from the rat in homologous regions of CA1 showed strong and prevalent theta modulation.
source: This contrasts with the strong and prevalent modulation seen using the same analyses methods applied to signal from the rat in homologous regions of CA1.
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of rat CA1 data using identical methods

claim: In rat and mouse hippocampal LFPs, theta activity (centered at 6–9 Hz) is most consistently present during activated cortical states.
source: In rat and mouse hippocampal LFPs, theta activity (centered at 6–9 Hz) is most consistently present during activated cortical states, that is, during alert aroused behaviors and REM sleep (Buzsáki, 2002; Colgin, 2013; Nuñez and Buño, 2021; Vanderwolf, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent hippocampal literature

claim: In rodents, theta gives way to SWRs and irregular slow activity during quiescence and NREM sleep.
source: In contrast, theta gives way to SWRs and irregular slow activity during quiescence and NREM sleep (Buzsáki, 2015; Buzsáki, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent sleep studies

claim: In rodents, theta 'nests' different frequencies of gamma in a phase-specific manner during active cortical states.
source: Further, theta 'nests' different frequencies of gamma in a phase-specific manner during these 'active' cortical states (Colgin and Moser, 2010; Colgin, 2016; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent theta-gamma coupling studies

claim: Most classes of cells in rodent CA1 are modulated by the theta rhythm.
source: And finally, most classes of cells in CA1 are modulated by the theta rhythm (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; Klausberger et al., 2003; Royer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent cellular electrophysiology studies

claim: Monkey CA1 LFPs show reliable, durable theta oscillations with peak frequencies at 6–9 Hz.
source: Monkey CA1 LFPs also show reliable, durable theta oscillations with peak frequencies at 6–9 Hz; however, where measured across states, they do not demonstrate the above characteristics of theta.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations of theta during rest/sleep

claim: Monkey CA1 theta oscillations do not demonstrate the characteristics of rodent theta when measured across states.
source: Monkey CA1 LFPs also show reliable, durable theta oscillations with peak frequencies at 6–9 Hz; however, where measured across states, they do not demonstrate the above characteristics of theta.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of behavioral state correlates between species

claim: Monkey CA1 theta oscillations show divergent brain-behavior coupling to that seen in rodents.
source: Instead, they show divergent brain-behavior coupling to that seen in rodents.
evidence: Inferred from the contrasting behavioral state correlates observed

claim: Where rest or sleep have been measured in primates, stronger, more durable theta field potential oscillations appear during quiescence and NREM sleep than during alert/task-on states or REM sleep.
source: Yet where rest or sleep have been measured, stronger, more durable theta field potential oscillations appear during quiescence and NREM sleep (or anesthetized states, Kleen et al., 2021) than during alert/task-on states or REM sleep (Bódizs et al., 2001; Cox et al., 2019; Moroni et al., 2007; Tamura et al., 2013; Uchida et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to primate and human sleep studies

claim: All tested frequencies had at least some units that were preferentially phase locked to them.
source: All tested frequencies had at least some units that were preferentially phase locked to them, but the most common preferred frequencies were roughly matching the 3–10 Hz, 20–30 Hz, and 60–150 Hz bands.
evidence: Supported by spike-field coherence analysis across frequencies

claim: The most common preferred frequencies for spike-field locking were roughly matching the 3–10 Hz, 20–30 Hz, and 60–150 Hz bands.
source: All tested frequencies had at least some units that were preferentially phase locked to them, but the most common preferred frequencies were roughly matching the 3–10 Hz, 20–30 Hz, and 60–150 Hz bands.
evidence: Supported by spike-field coherence analysis showing distribution of preferred frequencies

claim: Spike-field coherence in the theta frequency range was seen for microelectrode bundles including microwires in unspecified subregions of the human hippocampus.
source: Spike-field coherence in the theta frequency range was seen for microelectrode bundles including microwires in unspecified subregions of the human hippocampus (Rutishauser et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to human hippocampal study

claim: In freely moving macaque, higher gamma bands and delta bands were several times more likely to show spike-field coherence than theta.
source: Spike-field coherence in the theta frequency range was seen for microelectrode bundles including microwires in unspecified subregions of the human hippocampus (Rutishauser et al., 2010), and for recording sites estimated to be within the hippocampus proper of the freely moving macaque (Mao et al., 2021), though in the latter case, the higher gamma bands and delta bands were several times more likely to show SFC.
evidence: Supported by citation to macaque hippocampal study

claim: Spurious coherence may arise in response to nonrhythmic deflections.
source: Within the theta band, spurious coherence may arise in response to nonrhythmic deflections (Aru et al., 2015; de Cheveigné and Nelken, 2019; Jones, 2016; Vinck et al., 2022), such as the slow components of the SWR which is especially prominent in macaques and human (Hussin et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to methodological studies on spurious coherence

claim: The slow components of the SWR are especially prominent in macaques and humans.
source: Within the theta band, spurious coherence may arise in response to nonrhythmic deflections (Aru et al., 2015; de Cheveigné and Nelken, 2019; Jones, 2016; Vinck et al., 2022), such as the slow components of the SWR which is especially prominent in macaques and human (Hussin et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing SWRs in primates

claim: SWRs disproportionally influenced the 2–10 Hz band.
source: Indeed, we found that SWRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) disproportionally influenced the 2–10 Hz band (Figure 2B, D and E), whereas the gamma frequency range was largely unaffected.
evidence: Supported by analysis comparing spike-field coherence with and without SWR epochs

claim: The gamma frequency range was largely unaffected by SWR removal.
source: Indeed, we found that SWRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) disproportionally influenced the 2–10 Hz band (Figure 2B, D and E), whereas the gamma frequency range was largely unaffected.
evidence: Supported by analysis comparing spike-field coherence with and without SWR epochs

claim: The population activity during ripples typically includes 2–10× firing rate increases in nearly all cell types.
source: Because SWRs occur infrequently, it was somewhat surprising that SWR removal affected the overall results; however, the population activity during ripples typically includes 2–10× firing rate increases in nearly all cell types (Buzsáki, 2015; Hussin et al., 2020; Leonard et al., 2015; Skaggs et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing neural activity during SWRs

claim: Each ripple is likely contributing disproportionately to the spike-locked activity.
source: As such, each ripple is likely contributing disproportionately to the spike-locked activity.
evidence: Inferred from the high firing rates during SWRs despite their infrequent occurrence

claim: Visual and saccade-elicited responses in the hippocampus increase theta-band power without necessarily producing harmonic oscillations.
source: In addition, we know that visual (Katz et al., 2020; Rey et al., 2014; Roux et al., 2022) and saccade-elicited ('ERP-like') responses in the hippocampus (Hoffman et al., 2013; Jutras et al., 2009; Katz et al., 2022) increase theta-band power without necessarily producing harmonic oscillations.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on evoked responses in hippocampus

claim: The typical duration of sleep theta bouts would well exceed the SWR envelope.
source: The present results found residual coherence, and in addition, the typical duration of sleep theta bouts would well exceed the SWR envelope (as shown in Video 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4), therefore we consider the observed spectral peaks during rest likely reflect true oscillations and not simply collections of evoked transients.
evidence: Supported by analysis of theta bout durations shown in Video 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: The observed spectral peaks during rest likely reflect true oscillations and not simply collections of evoked transients.
source: The present results found residual coherence, and in addition, the typical duration of sleep theta bouts would well exceed the SWR envelope (as shown in Video 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4), therefore we consider the observed spectral peaks during rest likely reflect true oscillations and not simply collections of evoked transients.
evidence: Inferred from the duration of theta bouts and residual coherence after SWR removal

claim: The spike autocorrelogram is a more stringent measure of oscillatory modulation, not susceptible to LFP spectral analysis artifacts.
source: The spike autocorrelogram is a more stringent measure of oscillatory modulation, not susceptible to LFP spectral analysis artifacts.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of electrophysiological methods

claim: The <10 Hz range including the theta band failed to show clear examples of theta modulation in spike autocorrelograms.
source: The <10 Hz range including the theta band failed to show clear examples of theta modulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by spike autocorrelogram analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Even high firing rate cells, which should include 'theta-on' interneurons, failed to show theta modulation.
source: This was not simply due to low firing rates: even high firing rate cells, which should include 'theta-on' interneurons, failed to show theta modulation.
evidence: Supported by analysis of spike autocorrelograms across different firing rate cells

claim: The same analysis applied to units from a homologous region of rat CA1 showed a predominance of theta modulation.
source: Indeed, the same analysis applied to units from a homologous region of rat CA1 (Royer et al., 2010) showed a predominance of theta modulation (even after pooling functional cell types).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of rat CA1 data

claim: To observe spike timing regularity to field potentials in some primate studies, the aperiodic slow fluctuations in the LFP must first be warped to 'fit' one another, to create a pseudo-oscillation.
source: In such cases, to observe spike timing regularity to field potentials, the aperiodic – that is non oscillatory – slow fluctuations in the LFP must first be warped to 'fit' one another, to create a pseudo-oscillation (Bush and Burgess, 2020; Eliav et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2021; Qasim et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies using warping methods

claim: Slower oscillations at 1–4 Hz 'delta' band are more frequently correlated with spatial or associative memory effects.
source: Slower oscillations, or irregular low-frequency components at 1–4 Hz 'delta' band, are more frequently correlated with spatial or associative memory effects (Goyal et al., 2020; Vivekananda et al., 2021; Watrous et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to memory studies

claim: Gamma oscillations in rat and mouse CA1 comprise a wide high-frequency band initially 40–100 Hz but more recently 20 Hz or 30–100 Hz.
source: Gamma oscillations in rat and mouse CA1 comprise a wide high-frequency band (initially 40–100 Hz but more recently 20 Hz or 30–100 Hz) known for tight coupling within the theta oscillation (Bragin et al., 1995a; Buzsáki et al., 1983; Colgin and Moser, 2010; Colgin et al., 2009; Tort et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent gamma oscillation studies

claim: Rodent gamma oscillations are known for tight coupling within the theta oscillation.
source: Gamma oscillations in rat and mouse CA1 comprise a wide high-frequency band (initially 40–100 Hz but more recently 20 Hz or 30–100 Hz) known for tight coupling within the theta oscillation (Bragin et al., 1995a; Buzsáki et al., 1983; Colgin and Moser, 2010; Colgin et al., 2009; Tort et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent theta-gamma coupling studies

claim: The slower part of the gamma range (<~70 Hz) is decoupled from theta in macaque CA1.
source: We found that the slower part of the gamma range (<~70 Hz) is decoupled from theta.
evidence: Supported by cross-frequency coupling analyses

claim: Gamma power is seen as a relatively strong oscillation in monkeys and humans during REM sleep.
source: Consistent with this finding, gamma power is seen as a relatively strong oscillation in monkeys and humans during REM sleep (Cantero et al., 2003; Takeuchi et al., 2015; Tamura et al., 2013; Uchida et al., 2001), as in rodents.
evidence: Supported by citations to primate and human sleep studies

claim: Gamma oscillations are often associated with hippocampal processing in monkeys.
source: Gamma oscillations, when measured, are often associated with hippocampal processing (e.g. memory guided search, Leonard et al., 2015; Montefusco-Siegmund et al., 2017), and retrieval (Montefusco-Siegmund et al., 2017) or subsequent memory effects (Jutras et al., 2009) in monkeys
evidence: Supported by citations to monkey hippocampal studies

claim: A band-limited 20–40 Hz oscillation is seen in rodent CA1 during discrete item cueing or retrieval.
source: In addition, a band-limited 20–40 Hz oscillation is seen in rodent CA1 (and is synchronized with LEC, Igarashi et al., 2014) during discrete item cueing or retrieval such as in olfactory associative place and sequence learning (Allen et al., 2016; França et al., 2014; Lansink et al., 2016; Lopes-Dos-Santos et al., 2018), and when exploring novel environments (França et al., 2021; Trimper et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent behavioral studies

claim: The 20–40 Hz frequency band is associated with activation of the trisynaptic pathway (DG and CA3).
source: This frequency band is associated with activation of the trisynaptic pathway (DG and CA3, Colgin, 2016; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2021; Hsiao et al., 2016; Rangel et al., 2015), but is also a coherent oscillation between CA1 and LEC (Igarashi et al., 2014) implicating direct, temporoammonic pathways.
evidence: Supported by citations to circuit-level studies

claim: The 20–40 Hz frequency band is also a coherent oscillation between CA1 and LEC implicating direct, temporoammonic pathways.
source: This frequency band is associated with activation of the trisynaptic pathway (DG and CA3, Colgin, 2016; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2021; Hsiao et al., 2016; Rangel et al., 2015), but is also a coherent oscillation between CA1 and LEC (Igarashi et al., 2014) implicating direct, temporoammonic pathways.
evidence: Supported by citation to study showing CA1-LEC coherence

claim: Beta2/gamma coherence is seen in hippocampal-retrosplenial and hippocampal-mFPC oscillations in monkeys during object-scene associative memory.
source: Finally, beta2/gamma coherence is seen in hippocampal-retrosplenial and hippocampal-mFPC oscillations in monkeys during object-scene associative memory (Hussin et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to monkey memory study

claim: Theta oscillations are not prominent during awake behavior in macaque CA1.
source: The results of the current study show that theta oscillations are not prominent during awake behavior and do not couple with gamma, and thus, are not a good candidate for structuring possible gamma sub-bands.
evidence: Supported by power spectral and coupling analyses during active behaviors

claim: Theta oscillations do not couple with gamma in macaque CA1.
source: The results of the current study show that theta oscillations are not prominent during awake behavior and do not couple with gamma, and thus, are not a good candidate for structuring possible gamma sub-bands.
evidence: Supported by cross-frequency coupling analyses

claim: Theta is not a good candidate for structuring possible gamma sub-bands in macaque CA1.
source: The results of the current study show that theta oscillations are not prominent during awake behavior and do not couple with gamma, and thus, are not a good candidate for structuring possible gamma sub-bands.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of theta-gamma coupling observed

claim: Beta2/slow gamma oscillations constitute the chief, self-contained oscillation that arises during active exploration in the primate hippocampus.
source: Instead, beta2/slow gamma oscillations constitute the chief, self-contained oscillation that arises during active exploration in the primate hippocampus and stands as the most likely oscillation for organizing local dynamics during exploration.
evidence: Inferred from the prominence of beta2/gamma during active behaviors and its decoupling from theta

claim: Beta2/slow gamma stands as the most likely oscillation for organizing local dynamics during exploration in the primate hippocampus.
source: Instead, beta2/slow gamma oscillations constitute the chief, self-contained oscillation that arises during active exploration in the primate hippocampus and stands as the most likely oscillation for organizing local dynamics during exploration.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing beta2/gamma prominence during exploration
